start.text: A woman sits on a folded sack at the very end of the stage with her forearms on her knees, a sacking hood pulled up over her head and down over her shoulders. A long braid comes out of it over one shoulder, grey and black, and the end of it has gone silver.
She doesn't look round until you're nearly beside her, and then she looks at your hand first.
Came down the steps, though. Nobody comes down the steps but the Lamp, and the Lamp's knees gave out before I was grey.
Wenna Coll. Collier, near side. I had a hearth out along the cart road, before the road took to lying.
Told you somebody'd come down. Told you.
Told you somebody'd come down. Told you. In my cap and all.
You told me the boat'd come, Ottie Swale. You tell me a lot.

greet.text: Wenna hasn't moved. Out past the end of the stage the fog lies on the water, and she watches it as if it might open.

choice.text: What are you waiting for?
Why did you need a light of your own?
You've been counting days on the bollard.
The Spire's dark. The boat isn't coming.
Come up. Somebody came down for you: me.
Wait for it, then. I'll tell the Spire you're here.
Goodbye.

boat.text: The Spire's boat. Came in here every midwinter, under the cliff, for the keeper. Everybody our side knew it. Lamp went up the old road with a lantern once a winter and came back a week after with a new coal, and you don't get a coal off the Spire walking.
So there's a boat. And a boat from the Spire'll have lanterns aboard, more than it needs. A boat that size always has more than it needs.
I'll ask for one. That's all. One light of my own. Lamp couldn't spare one, and I don't blame it. It had a road to keep.

hearth.text: My clamp's out along the cart road, north of the wall. The night the light went, the road started lying. You know that. Everybody knows it now.

I walked out to my own clamp in the morning and came back into the clearing. Walked out again, came back into the clearing. Three times. I could smell it burning. My own smoke, and I couldn't find the fire under it.
She turns the end of her braid in her fingers, the silver part, and lets it go.
Proper light goes where things are. Lamp's lanterns don't lie, Hob says. So: a lantern. Then I go home.

days.text: Somebody has to. Ottie counts in sacks. Abe and Tolly count in arguments. Lamp counted winters on that bollard, thirty of them, and the last one's fresh. The boat came that winter. It came every winter.
I count days. When I get to a winter's worth, I'll know something.

dark.text: Lamp said that. Spires get lit again, I said. Somebody'll come in a boat when it is.
You've got the same light in your hand the Lamp had in its box. So somebody's lighting something, somewhere. You're the proof of it.
You tell her what Brother Aldous told you in Saltmarrow: put out, not went out.
Put out. Then somebody can put it back. Things that get put out get put back. That's what hands are for.

up.text: She looks at you a long time. Then past you, up, at the cliff and the wool lying on top of it, and the steps going up into it.
High on the cliff the Northing's lantern makes a gold place in the fog.
That's what I was waiting for, maybe. You don't say that to yourself, sitting on the end of a quay. You say boat. Boat's a better thing to wait for. It's got a shape.

You tell her what the Lamp keeps in its iron box: the last of the coal, a thumbnail of it, kept for the four. 'If they come back along the ridge, there should be a light at the end of it that knows their faces.'
It said that? For us? It never said that to us. It said no, and put the ladder down.
She gets up off the sack, folds it, and puts it under her arm. Then she pushes her hood back off her head, as if she'd only just noticed it was up.
Up. He said up. She said up. Up.

For once the Drays are moving the same way. Abe rakes the fire out and kicks the stones in over it, collier-fashion; Tolly takes the kettle off and then, after a look at it, puts it back down on its stone.
I'll leave the lantern on the bracket. For the boat. Somebody should be lit for it, if it comes.
Four. One, two, three, four. I'll count you up the steps. I'll count you every step.
Three. Three, and Ottie home. Four. I'll count you up the steps.

They go up the Keepers' steps the way they went, one at a time, Wenna first with the sack under her arm. The fog takes them a step at a time. Near the top, you think, one of them stops to look back down at the stage. Then the wool closes.
Tell the boat we went home. If it comes.

wait.text: She says it the way you'd say a word in a language you used to know.

Yes. You do that. Tell them there's colliers on the Northing's stage wanting lanterns, and how many. You can count; you've a light to count by. Tell them we're not proud. We'll take the ones with dents in.
There's a spring under the cliff and limpets on the stones. Colliers have lived on less. We'll be here when it comes.
Told you. Told you it's coming.
You told me the opposite of everything for forty years, Abe. You'd think one of them would come true by accident.
Waiting, then. I don't wait well. I'll learn.
Somebody's to count them. I'll count them. Morning and night.
Wenna sits back down on her sack at the end of the stage, and takes a nail out of her smock, and scratches a stroke on the bollard's cap.

waiting.text: Wenna is on the end of the stage, her nail in her hand. There are more strokes on the bollard than last time.
Not yet. You told them? Don't tell me if you haven't. I'd rather think you had.

choice.text: Come up, Wenna. It's not too late to go home.
Goodbye.

home.text: Wenna Coll stands by Hob's clamp with her hood pushed back and a Keeper's lantern held out in front of her by its bail, gold behind horn. She keeps lifting it a little, the way you'd lift a lantern to see a face.

The Lamp knew us. We came along the ridge in the dark and there it was at the bench, and it said my name before I'd said it. Thirty winters it never looked at us, I'd have said. It knew all four faces.
It broke the coal for us. The warm side. Said the cold side was no use to anybody and it'd keep it anyway.
Hob knew us. Didn't say a thing. Just counted. Four. Then sat down on his step like his legs had gone and slept where he sat.
Hob came up the steps behind us counting. He's stopped now. First time I've seen Hob Marl stop counting anything.
Hob looked at us like weather. Said it's always been just him, this side of the ridge. Said it kind. Well. We know him. That'll do to be going on with.
I'm going out along the cart road in the morning with this. To find my clamp. If it's lying, I'll know, now.

choice.text: Can I walk out with you in the morning?
Good luck, Wenna.

ask.text: She looks at you over the lantern a while, the way she looked at the sea off the end of the stage.
I walked out three times on my own and came back in here three times. Smelling my own smoke. Maybe it wants two.
First light, then. I'll be by the first mark past the wall, where the road starts. Bring your hand.

asked.text: Wenna Coll is sitting up by Hob's clamp with the lantern on her knee, not sleeping.
First light. By the first mark, by the wall. I'll not go without you; I said I wouldn't.

choice.text: First light.

first_light.text: Wenna Coll stands under the first waymark's lantern with her own held out at arm's length over the moss, the way you'd hold a lantern over water to see the bottom.
Morning. Near enough. It's always this colour in here.

choice.text: Where was your hearth?
How does a road lie?
Show me.
Not yet.

where.text: Out east of here. Bram's lads'll tell you the cart road runs straight from the wall to the ridge. It does now. It didn't.
It bent. Here, just past the first mark, east round the hollow, past my hearth, and back on north to the ridge. Forty years I walked that bend with a cart. It was the long way and it was the way.

lie.text: The night the Spire went out the road straightened itself. Like a man pulling his arm in. Didn't leave a mark. The ruts just went on straight, as if they always had.

I walked out to my clamp three times on the straight road and came back in here every time. Never found the fire. Could smell it, though. My own smoke, the whole way round. That's the lie: it doesn't stop you. It just doesn't take you there.

not_yet.text: I've waited since the Snuffing. I'll wait while you tie your boots.

show.text: She lowers the lantern to the moss east of the road. In its light there are two grooves under the green, a cart's width apart, going off between the pines where there's no road at all.
Your ember leans after the lantern. The ruts are there in your light too, now that you've seen them.
There. Proper light goes where things are. I said it would.
Stay in the light. It's lied to me three times. It can lie to you once.
You walk east behind her, off the road, on ruts nobody's used since the Snuffing.

at_hearth.text: Wenna Coll stands by the sunk grey hump of her clamp with the lantern held out over it, looking at it the way you'd look at somebody asleep.
All this while. It was right here all this while.
You looked at it. Burned clean through, didn't it. Nobody to shut a vent, and it went all the way down and never once broke out. Best burn I ever had. I wasn't there for it.

choice.text: What was it like, when the road started lying?
Where does the road go from here?
What will you do with your light?
Hang it on the bend's waymark. Let the road be a road again.
Keep it by your own door. You went a long way for a light of your own.
Goodbye.

that_night.text: I'd just lit her. That clamp. Shut the vents for the night and gone in, and the Spire went, and in the morning I came out of the clearing, where I'd been for salt, and the road was straight.
I knew where I'd left her. A collier always knows where her fire is. Didn't help. Knowing where a thing is and getting there aren't the same, it turns out. Nobody tells you that.

north.text: She lifts the lantern toward the north side of the hollow. The ruts go on that way between the grey pines and thin out into the moss and the fog, and then there isn't anything.
On north, round the back of the hollow, and back onto the road under the ridge. The other end of the bend. Nobody's found that end either. I'd not go looking.

A road's only a road if people can find each other on it. This one's mine and nobody else's, now. The camp side of the wall it's a straight line, and Bram's lads go straight up it to the ridge, and they'd never once find me.

light.text: I wanted a light of my own. Sat on a quay counting days for one. Proper light goes where things are; I said that and it's true. It brought me here.
She looks back along the ruts to where the bend's waymark stands in the fog, its hook empty.

That's a Keepers' mark at the bend. The Lamp's lot set it, before my mother's time, so a cart'd know to turn. Hang a Keeper's coal on it and the bend's a road again, I'd think. That's what the marks are for. Anybody'd find me. Anybody'd find anybody.
Or I keep it by my door. My own light, at my own hearth, like I wanted. And the road goes on lying about me, and I don't mind. Colliers don't, much.
You walked out with me. You say.

road.text: She walks back along the ruts to the bend's waymark and reaches up and hangs the lantern on its hook. It swings once and settles, gold behind horn.

The fog leans back off the bend the way it leans off the woods' other marks: down the ruts to the straight road one way, up through the hollow to the hearth the other, and on north a stone's throw, until the ruts go into the thick. You can see the whole bend from the waymark. It's a road.
There. Now it's a road. Somebody'll come along it. That's what roads are for. Bram's lads with their straight line, maybe. I'll sell them charcoal to their faces.
I'll not have a light of my own. I'll have the road's. That's more, I think. I'll have to see.
She goes back to her hut and sits down on the seat by the door for the first time since the Snuffing, and says nothing at all for a while, and then gets up and puts the fire in.

bend_road.text: Wenna Coll sits on the seat by her hut door with the fire in behind her and her big hands on her knees. Down the ruts the bend's lantern burns on its waymark.
Wenna Coll is at her clamp with the rake, stooped into it, the charcoal coming out black onto the moss a stroke at a time. Down the ruts the bend's lantern burns on its waymark.

Hob came along it this morning with his cart, the long way, to see. Stood at the waymark a long time. 'Road's a road again,' he says. 'Said I'd come in when it was. Said that once.' Didn't know it was my road he meant. Neither did he.

Hob came along it this morning with his cart, to see what the light was. Didn't know me from Abe. Said he'd never seen a hearth out here, and he's been this side of the ridge all his life. Well. He's seen one now.
I'll take my own sacks down the bend to the gap in my own cart, when there's sacks. Bram Kettle can cut himself a new row.
I'll put another clamp up when the cordwood's dry. A collier's not a collier sitting.

choice.text: Goodbye, Wenna.

bend_hearth.text: Wenna Coll sits on the seat by her hut door under her own lantern, gold behind horn on its forked stake, the fire in behind her.
Wenna Coll is at her clamp with the rake, stooped into it, the charcoal coming out black onto the moss a stroke at a time. Her own lantern burns by the hut door behind her.
Still here. The road's still lying, down there. Bram's lads go straight past and never know. I hear their cart some mornings. I don't call out.
I took my first sacks down to Hob's clearing myself. Walked in under his lanterns and stood by his cart till he saw me. 'Wenna,' he says. Didn't count. Just said it.
I took my first sacks down to Hob's clearing myself and stood by his cart till he saw me. Asked who I was. I told him. He'll forget, out here. I'll tell him again. I've time.
I'll put another clamp up when the cordwood's dry. By my own light. I said I would.

choice.text: Goodbye, Wenna.

keep_it.text: Mine, then. I said that on a quay every day. I meant it.

She cuts a forked stake from the cordwood with the hatchet off her hut's wall, drives it in by the door with the back of it, and hangs the lantern in the fork. Gold behind horn, at the height of her shoulder. The hut looks lived in at once.
Down the ruts the bend's waymark stands in the fog with its hook empty. From here you can hardly see it.
Let the road lie. I know where I am. Anybody wants me, they can ask Hob, and Hob can't tell them. Suits a collier.
My sacks'll go down with his cart. He'll find me. He'll find me because I'll go and stand where he is.
She sits down on the seat by the door for the first time since the Snuffing, under her own light, and after a while she gets up and puts the fire in.
